text: You know the interface now. Time to actually build something. This lesson, we connect to real data and get two visuals on the canvas — start to finish.

Here's where this is all headed eventually: a title, a few charts, a map, arranged on one page that tells a story at a glance. We're not building all of that today — formatting, DAX, and slicers each get their own lessons later. Today, just two pieces: getting data in, and getting a visual out.

Every report starts the same way. On the Home ribbon, select Get data. This one button is the front door to dozens of connectors — Excel, SQL databases, web pages, and more. Chapter 2 covers all of them. Today, we're using Excel.
Choose Excel from the list, connect, and point Power BI at your workbook.

Power BI shows you every table it found inside the file, in a window called Navigator. Check the ones you want, and select Load. Once it's loaded, look at the Fields pane — your table and its columns are sitting right there, ready to use.

Now the fun part. Drag a numeric field — profit, sales, anything with numbers — onto a blank spot on the canvas. Power BI draws a chart automatically. Drag a second field, like a date, onto that same visual, and it redraws to break your numbers out across time. No chart-drawing, no formulas — just fields, dragged.

Try it again with a different kind of field — a country or region — and Power BI might hand you a map instead of a bar chart, sized by whatever number you add next. Same exact mechanic every time: drag fields, let Power BI guess, then pick the visual type you actually want from the Visualizations pane.

Data in, two visuals out, and saved with Control-S. That's a real Power BI report, built by you. In the next lesson, we zoom back out and walk through the entire five-step workflow this whole course is built around. See you there.
